open-question.question: Gurita for VS Code is to call a recipe an "action" where the user fires it and an "action recipe" in the Settings window, while the recipe files, their `## Recipes` heading, and the `gurita.ownRecipesFile` setting keep the name "recipe". Which word do the user-read texts that are neither a firing point nor the Settings window use: the mission page's failure line `The recipes could not be read.`, error notifications such as `No recipe is named <name>.`, the hover text `Recipe: <name>` on the side-bar view's two mission-starting rows, the description of the `gurita.ownRecipesFile` setting, and the extension's README prose?
open-question.alternative: None of these texts changes. The page's failure line stays `The recipes could not be read.`, the error notifications stay as they read today (`No recipe is named <name>.`, the looped run's `No recipe is a single-task line: …`, the preview's `… of the recipe <name> …`), the mission-starting rows' hover keeps `Recipe: <name>`, the `gurita.ownRecipesFile` description keeps "your own recipe file, read beside the shipped recipes", and the listing README keeps "recipe" in its prose. Only the firing points and the Settings window take the new words. No string, test expectation, or README passage changes beyond what the goal already requires, and every text outside the buttons keeps matching the recipe files, their `## Recipes` heading, and the setting's key, which still say "recipe". The user meets two words for one thing on the same surfaces: a mission page headed "Actions" shows `The recipes could not be read.` beneath it, a click on an action can raise `No recipe is named <name>.`, and nothing in these texts says that an action and a recipe are the same thing.

Every one of these texts calls the thing "action": `The actions could not be read.`, `No action is named <name>.` and the other notifications likewise, the hover `Action: <name>`, and the README's prose. The word "recipe" survives only where a text names a file or key that keeps it — "recipe file", the `## Recipes` heading, `gurita.ownRecipesFile` — so the setting's description reads along the lines of "the path of your own recipe file, whose actions are read beside the shipped ones". Whatever the user reads at run time or in the documentation uses the word the buttons use, so "recipe" appears only as the name of a file format, which is exactly the split the goal draws. The Settings window's "action recipe" becomes the one place a compound word stands, the README must explain why the files holding actions are recipe files, and the broadest set of strings, tests, and some 150 README mentions changes.

Every one of these texts uses the Settings window's compound "action recipe": `The action recipes could not be read.`, `No action recipe is named <name>.` and the other notifications likewise, the hover `Action recipe: <name>`, the setting description "your own recipe file, holding action recipes read beside the shipped ones", and the README's prose. One term bridges the two names the goal fixes — it contains "action", the button word, and "recipe", the file word — so every non-button text reads as the Settings window does and the README needs no separate statement linking the two. The compound is long in the short texts (a hover, a one-line failure under an "Actions" heading, a notification), and the page then shows "Actions" over a failure about "action recipes", a third surface wording beside the button's.

alternative.id: Action at run time, recipe in docs

open-question.alternative: The texts the user meets while working with missions say "action": the page's failure line, the error notifications, and the mission-starting rows' hover (`The actions could not be read.`, `No action is named <name>.`, `Action: <name>`). The texts that describe configuration keep "recipe": the `gurita.ownRecipesFile` description and the README's prose, the README stating once that each recipe in a recipe file is shown as an action where it is fired and as an action recipe in the Settings window. Each text uses the word of the layer it belongs to — the runtime texts match the buttons they stand beside, and the setting and README match the files, heading, and key they describe — and the large README changes by one explanatory sentence rather than throughout. The vocabulary rule is per text and must be judged for every new string (is it a run-time or a documentation text?), and a README reader looking for the "Actions" list the page shows finds it described as recipes throughout.

alternative.id: Action at run time, action recipe in docs

open-question.alternative: The page's failure line, the error notifications, and the mission-starting rows' hover say "action", as in the option above, while the `gurita.ownRecipesFile` description and the README's prose use the Settings window's "action recipe", the README naming the file that holds them the recipe file. The configuration texts read exactly as the Settings window, the one configuration surface, does, and the runtime texts read as the buttons do, so each text matches the surface it sits nearest to. Three words stand in the extension's texts (action, action recipe, and recipe for the file), the README's prose changes throughout as in the all-action option and grows wordier, and the per-text rule must still be judged for every new string.

open-question.question: The shipped recipe `Requirements iteration` is to be renamed "Approve all standing recommendations and review again", a name that describes the answer sweep followed by one review pass. Its `default` variant runs the answer sweep, a review pass, the alternatives pass, and an interactive recommendation pass, and its `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` variant runs a review pass, the alternatives pass, the recommendation pass, and then the answer sweep. Do both variants keep their lines unchanged under the new name, or are their lines changed to match what the name says?
open-question.alternative: Both variants keep every line, its order, harness, model, effort, and interactive marker exactly as they stand: the `default` variant still runs the answer sweep, a review pass, the alternatives pass, and the interactive recommendation pass, and the `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` variant still runs the Antigravity review pass, the alternatives pass, the headless recommendation pass, and then the answer sweep. Only the `###` heading changes to "Approve all standing recommendations and review again". No chain behaves differently, so a user's habit and every test asserting the lines (`recipes.test.ts` checks the mixed-agent variant's lines) stay as they are, and the `default` variant, the one most runs use, already opens with exactly the two steps the name states, its trailing annotation passes being what prepares the next round's standing recommendations. The `Mixed-agent` variant contradicts the name it is listed under: it reviews first and approves last, approving the recommendations it formed in the same run rather than standing ones, and runs no review after approving, so a button reading "Approve all standing recommendations and review again" runs the reverse order when that variant is selected.

The `default` variant keeps its lines unchanged. The `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` variant keeps its four lines, harnesses, models, and efforts but is reordered to the `default` variant's pass order: the Claude Code answer sweep first, then the Antigravity review pass, the alternatives pass, and the headless recommendation pass last. Both variants then run the same chain the name describes and differ only in which agent runs which pass, which is what a variant of one recipe is meant to be, and each starts by approving the recommendations standing from the previous round before reviewing again. The variant changes behaviour for anyone using it: it no longer ends with every pick recorded but leaves fresh recommendations standing for the next run, so its current trait of a fully headless round that closes on the sweep is lost, and the test asserting its lines and the README paragraph describing its order must change with it.

Both variants are cut to the two passes the name states, the answer sweep followed by one review pass (`default` on Claude Code, the `Mixed-agent` variant with its Antigravity review line), and the alternatives and recommendation passes move out into a new shipped chain of their own that annotates the open questions, so a round becomes two recipe runs. Every line under the new name is exactly what the name says, in both variants, and the annotation passes become runnable on their own, which no shipped recipe offers today outside `First run`. A review round that took one click now takes two, and a user who runs only the renamed recipe gets questions with no alternatives or picks, so its next run has nothing standing to approve; the mission also gains a shipped recipe the tracker never asked for, with its own `Stage:` line, name, and tests, and the page at the additional review round no longer lists the renamed recipe alone.

The `default` variant keeps its lines unchanged and stays the renamed recipe's only variant. The `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` chain leaves the renamed recipe with its lines unchanged and becomes a shipped recipe of its own, under `Stage: additional review round` and a name that states its own order (review, annotate, then approve). No line of either chain changes, and each name is truthful for the lines beneath it, so neither chain's behaviour nor the name has to give way. It reverses the earlier recipe-variants decision that the mixed-agent chain is a variant and no recipe of its own (`recipes.test.ts` asserts that), puts a second button on the page at the additional review round, adds a recipe name the mission must choose, and moves a user's remembered selection of that variant onto a different recipe, conditional on how the stored-state question settles state keyed by the old name.

The `default` variant keeps its lines unchanged and becomes the renamed recipe's only variant, and the `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` variant is removed from `gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md` altogether, with no replacement. The renamed recipe then holds only a chain that runs what its name says, with the fewest edits and no new recipe or reordered behaviour to explain. It removes the only shipped chain variant with an Antigravity line, from which the Settings window reads part of Antigravity's model and effort lists (`harnessLists.test.ts`), and the one shipped example of a mixed-harness chain, so users of that variant lose it, their stored selection of it conditional on how the stored-state question settles.

open-question.question: Gurita for VS Code keys a user's stored variants (`~/.gurita/variants.json`), picked defaults, and remembered variant selections by recipe name, and lists stored variants of a name no recipe file holds as an own recipe. Once the shipped recipe `Requirements iteration` carries its new name, "Approve all standing recommendations and review again", what happens to the state a user stored under the old name?
open-question.alternative: No migration and no alias: the variant store format, `overlayVariantStore`, `variantEdits.ts`, and the `workspaceState` selections stay unchanged, and state stored under `Requirements iteration` is read as it stands. Stored variants under the old name, stored copies of its `default` or mixed-agent variant included, form a recipe called `Requirements iteration` in the own group, which declares no `Stage:` and so is listed on every mission page. A hiding record or picked default under the old name matches no variant, so the renamed recipe shows every shipped variant and opens on its first. A remembered selection is kept only while that orphan recipe still lists the variant it names, and is otherwise dropped as one naming a gone variant. The listing README says that nothing carries stored state over to the new name, as it already says for the one-block variants renamed `default`, and the user moves it by hand in the Settings window. No code to write or test, and it follows the recorded precedent: when the one-block variants were renamed `default` (`751ed789`), no migration was added and the README said that nothing renames what was stored under the old name. It also matches the plugin's rule of answering to its current names only. A user who customised the recipe finds their copies and further variants under a stale-named own recipe that is listed on every step's page, while the renamed recipe has lost their hidden variants and picked default. Moving them back takes manual Settings-window work, since the window has no move between recipes. How confusing a stale copy is depends on whether the renamed recipe's lines change, which a sibling question decides.

A one-time migration writes the user's state over to the new name. When the extension activates, or on the first store read, it rewrites `~/.gurita/variants.json`: every `variants`, `hidden`, and `defaults` record whose recipe is `Requirements iteration`, and every `copies.recipe` or `from.recipe` reference naming it, is renamed to "Approve all standing recommendations and review again". Each project's `workspaceState` selection keys under the old name are renamed the same way as each workspace opens. The migration runs only while no recipe file holds a `### Requirements iteration` of its own, so a user's own recipe of that name keeps its state. A record that would collide with one already standing under the new name is left where it is. The README and changelog state that the migration happens. The user's customisations follow the recipe without the user doing anything: copies, further variants, hidden variants, the picked default, and remembered dropdown selections all land on the renamed recipe. After that the files hold only the current name, so every reader and editor works unchanged. The extension then rewrites a user's file on its own, with migration code, its collision rule, and tests that must be kept or retired later. This breaks the precedent of shipping no migration. A stored copy carried over keeps its old lines and stands in for the shipped variant, so if the sibling question changes the renamed recipe's lines, the user silently keeps the old chain under the new name.

alternative.id: Read the old name as an alias

open-question.alternative: No file is written: the reader treats the old name as an alias. Wherever the store is laid over the recipes (`overlayVariantStore`), wherever the Settings window lists and edits variants, and wherever selections are read, records and `workspaceState` keys naming `Requirements iteration` are read as belonging to "Approve all standing recommendations and review again". The alias applies only while no recipe file holds a recipe of the old name. New edits are written under the new name, and the old records stay in the files. The user's state follows the recipe and nothing in the user's files is rewritten behind their back, so going back to an earlier extension version still finds the state where that version left it. The alias lives permanently in every read and edit path: the overlay, `variantEdits.ts`, the Settings listing, and the three selection maps. A stored record can then be named two ways, so edits, deletions, resets, and duplicate-name checks have to treat old-name and new-name records as one recipe, and the store holds mixed names indefinitely. Like a migration, it carries stale copies onto the new name if the sibling question changes the recipe's lines.

open-question.question: The question card's "Answer with recommendation" button is to be removed from Gurita for VS Code. Does its shipped button recipe, `answer-open-question-with-recommendation`, leave `gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md` and the Settings window with it, or stay there with no button running it? Stored variants of a name no recipe file holds are listed today as an own recipe.

On a question card of Gurita for VS Code, each alternative's "Answer with this alternative" button and its arrow-only variant dropdown stand on one line with the alternative's id. The button is to stop being drawn as a one-line button, with the variant it will run stated after its title. What layout replaces that line: where do the button, the variant's name, and the dropdown stand relative to the alternative's id and text, and is the dropdown kept?

The question card of Gurita for VS Code is to draw text between backticks as code in the question, the pick's rationale, and each alternative's text, advantages, and drawbacks. The same mission starts drawing four more texts that are written as Markdown: the mission's goal in the mission page's introduction, each remaining task's brief, each completed task's verified bar, and a finished mission's summary. How much Markdown is rendered in those four texts: none, backtick spans as code only, or more of it, such as paragraphs, lists, and emphasis?
open-question.alternative: None of the four texts renders any Markdown: the goal, each brief, each verified bar, and each finished mission's summary are set through `textContent` as the card's texts are today, with their line breaks kept as written, so a bar's or summary's `- ` bullets stand as typed lines and backticks, asterisks, and blank lines show literally. The question card alone draws backtick spans as code. Needs no rendering code and no new failure mode at all. Every text shows exactly as the file or commit holds it, and nothing a text contains can ever be misread as markup. The same page draws a file name in backticks as code on a question card and as literal backticks in the goal, a brief, or a bar shown a few lines away. The four texts are the ones most full of backticked paths and commands, and the goal's paragraphs and the bars' bullets show only as raw lines.

The four texts are drawn by the same inline renderer the question card uses, built through DOM calls with no `innerHTML`: text between backticks becomes a code element and everything else stays plain text, with line breaks kept as written. A bar's or summary's `- ` bullets and the goal's blank lines therefore show as typed lines, not as a list or paragraphs. No other Markdown is read. One small renderer serves every text the page draws, so the card and the four new texts render alike. It renders the one construct these texts use most, paths and commands in backticks, at almost no extra cost and with no added risk. The texts' block structure stays raw. Verified bars and finished-mission summaries are bullet lists by contract, so they show as hyphen-led lines rather than lists. A multi-paragraph goal is separated only by blank lines, which reads roughly in the page's introduction. How much this matters depends on how much of a long goal the introduction shows, which is the long-goal sibling question's to settle.

alternative.id: Code spans, paragraphs, and bullet lists

open-question.alternative: A hand-written renderer built through DOM calls, with no `innerHTML` and no dependency, reads the block shapes the four texts' formats actually hold. Blank-line-separated paragraphs become paragraphs, consecutive `- ` lines become a bulleted list, and text between backticks becomes code inside either. Emphasis, links, headings, numbered lists, and every other construct stay plain text. The question card keeps its backtick-only drawing, which the same renderer gives for its single-paragraph texts. It covers every structure the formats define (the bar's and the summary's bullets, the goal's paragraphs, the brief's sentences with their code spans). It is still small enough to test fully against the stand-in DOM of the page tests and to keep free of injected markup. A second, larger parser lives in the page script and must be kept right, including the edge cases of a bullet continued onto a second line and a backtick span crossing a line break. Any author who writes emphasis or a numbered list sees it literally. The four texts render differently from the card wherever a card text ever holds a list.

The same hand-written, DOM-built renderer as the paragraphs-and-lists option, extended to inline emphasis and strong text (`*`/`_` and `**`/`__`) beside code spans. Links, headings, numbered lists, and the rest of Markdown stay plain text. It renders the inline styling an author is most likely to reach for in a goal or a summary. It still adds no dependency and sets no HTML string on the page. Emphasis is the hardest part of Markdown to parse correctly by hand. These texts are dense with globs, paths, and identifiers such as `**/mission_*/requirements.md` and `snake_case` names, and a hand parser mistakes their asterisks and underscores for emphasis wherever they stand outside backticks. That adds a misrendering risk for styling the workflow's formats never ask for.

alternative.id: Full Markdown through VS Code's renderer

open-question.alternative: The four texts are rendered as full Markdown by the editor's built-in Markdown extension: the host runs its `markdown.api.render` command on each text and sends the resulting HTML to the page, which sets it through `innerHTML` inside the page shell, with the page's stylesheet giving the elements their look. Every construct the editor's preview renders is rendered, including links, headings, and numbered lists. Complete, standard rendering with no parser of the extension's own and no new package. The texts look exactly as the editor's own Markdown preview shows them. It makes the page depend on a built-in extension that a user can disable, so the extension needs a fallback for when the command is missing. It adds an asynchronous host-side step to every redraw and the extension's first HTML-string insertion, which needs sanitizing and checking against the page's content security policy. Links in the HTML need their own handling inside a webview, and the page tests' stand-in DOM can no longer check the rendering.

alternative.id: Full Markdown through a bundled library

open-question.alternative: The four texts are rendered as full Markdown by a Markdown library (such as markdown-it) added as the extension's first runtime dependency. Because the build is `tsc` with no bundler, the library ships in the VSIX and runs either on the host, with its HTML sent to the page, or as a script the page loads under its nonce. The output is set through `innerHTML` with HTML input disabled or sanitized. Complete, standard, synchronous rendering that is fully under the extension's control, with no reliance on another extension being enabled and the same output on every machine. It ends the extension's dependency-free runtime. It adds packaging work for a project built with no bundler (shipping `node_modules` or copying the library into `bundled/`), a third-party package to audit and keep updated, and the HTML-insertion and webview link-handling concerns of any full renderer, all for constructs the four texts' formats barely use.

open-question.question: A mission page of Gurita for VS Code is to open with an introduction showing the mission's title and its goal above the workflow diagram. A goal read from `requirements.md` can run to several paragraphs. How much of a long goal does the introduction show, and can the reader expand or collapse it?
open-question.alternative: The introduction shows the whole `## Goal` body, every paragraph, beneath the title, at its full height, with no expand or collapse control and no limit on its length. The simplest form to build and test against the stand-in DOM: no toggle, no clamp, and no saved state, and the reader never misses part of the goal; the goals recorded so far in this scope run from about 90 to 170 words, mostly one paragraph, so in practice the introduction stays a few lines tall. A goal that does run to several paragraphs pushes the workflow diagram, the action buttons, and the panes below the fold on every opening of the page, and nothing lets the reader shrink it.

The introduction shows the goal inside a box of fixed maximum height, a few lines tall; a goal longer than the box scrolls inside it, and there is no expand or collapse control. The page below the introduction stands at the same place whatever the goal's length, and the whole goal stays readable on the page without any control or saved state. A nested scroll area inside a scrolling webview is awkward to read and to scroll past with the mouse wheel or keyboard, and nothing but a cut-off line shows the reader that more of the goal is hidden.

The introduction shows the goal clamped to its first few lines, with an ellipsis where it is cut, and no expand control on the page; a link beside it opens the mission's `requirements.md` in the editor, where the whole goal is read. The introduction keeps a fixed small height, the page gains no toggle or saved state, and the link gives the reader the goal in its full context, beside the decisions it led to. Reading the rest of the goal takes the reader off the page into an editor tab, and the extension gains a new command path that opens a mission file, which it has none of today.

The introduction shows the goal clamped to its first few lines, with a Show more control that expands it to the whole goal and a Show less control that clamps it again; the control appears only when the goal is longer than the clamp, and the goal is clamped again on every load of the page. A short goal shows whole with no control, a long one never pushes the page down unasked, and the whole goal is one click away on the page itself; with no saved state the page script's `setState` record gains nothing. Whether the goal overflows the clamp must be measured after layout, which the stand-in DOM the page tests run against cannot measure, so the control's presence is hard to test; and a reader who always wants the whole goal expands it again on every opening.

The introduction shows the goal clamped to its first few lines, with a Show more / Show less control appearing only when the goal overflows the clamp, collapsed by default, and the expanded or collapsed state saved with the page's `setState` beside its mission path and question positions, so it comes back when the window is reopened or restored. A reader's choice holds per mission window across hides, reloads, and restarts, so the goal is expanded once by someone who wants it and stays out of the way for someone who does not. It adds a field to the page's saved state and its restore path on top of the overflow measurement the reset form already needs, more to build and test for a goal that is in practice a single paragraph.

The introduction shows the goal's first paragraph whole, and when the goal holds more paragraphs a Show more / Show less control reveals and hides the rest; the cut falls at the first blank line of the `## Goal` body rather than at a line count, and it is collapsed on every load. Whether the control appears is decided from the text alone, with no layout measurement, so it is fully testable against the stand-in DOM, and the cut never falls mid-sentence. The recorded goals are mostly one paragraph of up to about 170 words, so the cut rarely shortens anything and a long single-paragraph goal still shows at full height; where paragraphs are drawn as such depends on how much Markdown the goal is rendered with, which the Markdown-in-new-texts question owns.

The introduction shows the whole goal by default, with a Show less control that clamps it to its first few lines and a Show more control that restores it; the control appears only when the goal overflows the clamp, and the goal is shown whole again on every load. A first-time reader of a mission sees the whole goal with nothing hidden, while a reader working on the page can still shrink it out of the way. A long goal still pushes the diagram and actions down on every opening, which is the case the control exists for, and it carries the same post-layout overflow measurement as the clamped forms.

The introduction shows the mission's title alone by default, with one control beside it that shows and hides the whole goal beneath it, collapsed on every load. The introduction is one line tall whatever the goal's length, and the control is always present, so it needs no overflow measurement and is decided and tested from the text alone. The page no longer says what the mission is for before anything else, which is what the tracker entry adding the introduction asks of it, unless the reader opens the goal every time.

open-question.question: A mission page of Gurita for VS Code is to offer "Ask in mission context" at every step of the workflow, and no shipped recipe runs the `ask-in-mission-context` skill today. Where does the action stand on the page: in the list of recipe buttons, as a shipped recipe that declares no `Stage:`, or as a fixed-name button outside that list, as New task is?
open-question.alternative: The action is a chain recipe that `gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md` ships under `## Recipes`, named "Ask in mission context", with no `Stage:` line and one line invoking `ask-in-mission-context --mission <path>`. It stands in the mission page's list of recipe buttons with the other recipes, drawn like them with its variant dropdown and, once recipes carry one, its own description. The reader and the page stay as they are: `stageRecipes` already keeps every undeclared recipe at every step. No `BUTTON_RECIPES` key, host handler, or page message is added, and the Settings window lists it as an ordinary action recipe whose variants an own recipe of the same name can extend. Undeclared recipes are already listed at every step, so the action is available at every step with no new code path. It is a recipe like the chains beside it, so its variants, harness lines, models, and description go through the existing recipe machinery and tests unchanged. Recipe-list buttons fill only `<path>` (`PAGE_PLACEHOLDERS`), and a variant holding any other known placeholder is silently left off. So the line cannot carry the user's question unless the question is typed inside the session it opens, or the recipe list learns to ask for values. That axis belongs to the sibling question on the ask question's input. The action would also sit among chains that move the workflow forward, though it changes nothing. And every variant falls out of the list when its harness is disabled, so "always available" holds only while at least one variant's harness is enabled.

The action is a fixed-name button outside the recipe list, labelled "Ask in mission context", standing in the same row as New task, which becomes the page's row of mission-wide actions above the two pane headers. It runs a shipped button recipe named by its skill, `ask-in-mission-context`, entered in `BUTTON_RECIPES`, kept out of the recipe list by name, and listed in the Settings window as a button recipe under the "Run by a button outside the recipe list" note. Like New task, it has an arrow-only variant dropdown of its own and a host handler that fills whatever values its line holds. It groups the two actions that do not depend on the step and that start from text the user brings. It reuses `fixedEntry` and the button-recipe path that New task already proves. The button can fill a placeholder of its own, so the question can be passed in, whichever way the input sibling settles, without changing what recipe-list buttons fill. It adds a new `BUTTON_RECIPES` key, a page message type, a host handler, a shipped button recipe, and tests across the page and Settings window. The button stands below the recipe list and any looped run's preview, so on a long page it is further from the top than the diagram's own recipes.

alternative.id: Fixed button in a top row

open-question.alternative: The action is a fixed-name button outside the recipe list, labelled "Ask in mission context", standing in a row of its own at the top of the page, between the introduction (title and goal) and the workflow diagram. It runs a shipped button recipe named `ask-in-mission-context`, entered in `BUTTON_RECIPES`, kept out of the recipe list by name, and listed in the Settings window as a button recipe, with an arrow-only variant dropdown of its own and a host handler that fills whatever values its line holds. New task keeps its own row where it stands. It is the first action the page shows at every step, directly under the mission's goal it asks about, so the reader never has to scroll past the step-specific recipes and panes to find it. As a fixed button it can fill a placeholder of its own for the question, without changing what recipe-list buttons fill. It has the same code cost as any fixed button (a `BUTTON_RECIPES` key, a message type, a handler, a shipped button recipe, tests), plus a new row in the page's stack. The two step-independent fixed buttons, Ask and New task, then stand at opposite ends of the page instead of together. A button above the diagram also pushes the diagram, and the reserved space for the waiting indicator, further down the page.

open-question.question: The `ask-in-mission-context` skill takes the user's question as its argument. When "Ask in mission context" is fired from a mission page of Gurita for VS Code, is the question typed before the run starts or inside the session the run opens, and is the run headless or interactive?
open-question.alternative: The question is typed before the run starts, through the extension's input-box path (`askValues`) as a required value that refuses an empty entry, as the issue description of `discuss-new-task` is today, and the action's line is an interactive one (a bare `claude "/gurita:ask-in-mission-context --mission <path> <question>" … # interactive`), so the session opens on the answer and stays open for follow-up questions. Matches the skill as written: its first answer arrives without a further prompt, its step 3 expects follow-ups that re-ground in the files, and its step 4 hand-off offers (`/submit-task`, `/discuss-open-question`, `/complete-task`) can be taken up in the same session, while the runner reads no verdict from an interactive line, so the run ends without a false stop. The mission page stays disabled for as long as the conversation stands, since a run blocks every action button until its terminal closes, so a quick look-up holds the page until the person exits the session; and the question goes through the one-line box unless the multi-line input sibling supplies a larger one.

The question is typed before the run starts in an input box that accepts an empty value, as the optional discussion note of `discuss-open-question` is today: a typed question is passed as the skill's argument, and an empty box passes none, so the skill gives its brief orientation to the mission (goal, what is done, what is left) and invites a question. The line is interactive, and the conversation continues in the session either way. One action covers both uses the skill supports, a specific question answered at once and an orientation when the person has none ready, with follow-ups and hand-off offers available in the session in both cases. An Enter pressed on an empty box by accident starts a full orientation run rather than nothing, and the page stays disabled while the session stands, as in every interactive form; it also adds `question` to the optional placeholders, a second exception beside `note`.

No value is asked before the run: firing the action starts an interactive session at once with the skill invoked on `--mission <path>` alone, so the skill opens with its orientation and invites a question, which the person types in the terminal, as many as they like. One click and no dialog, the question typed in the terminal with no length limit and no dependence on how the extension's input box is built, and the orientation gives the person a grounded starting point before they ask. Every use pays for an orientation pass, the skill's grounding reads included, before the person's actual question is answered, and the page stays disabled while the session stands; a person who knew their question waits for an answer to one they did not ask.

The question is typed before the run starts as a required value, and the action's line is headless (`claude -p "/gurita:ask-in-mission-context --mission <path> <question>" …`): the answer prints in the run's terminal, which then waits for a keypress and closes, with no follow-up. The shortest hold on the page: one question, one printed answer, and the terminal closed by a keypress, which suits a quick look-up from any step and matches the headless form of every other button recipe that takes a typed value, such as `answer-open-question`. The skill prints no fixed console line, so the runner's check finds no success or no-op line in the print and reports every run as a stopped chain, unless the runner or the action learns an exception; and the skill's follow-ups and hand-off offers are dead ends, since a second question means a second run and its own full grounding.

The question is typed before the run starts as a required value, and the action carries two variants chosen through its variant dropdown: an interactive one, the default, which keeps the session open for follow-ups, and a headless one, which prints the answer and closes on a keypress. The person chooses per use between a quick printed answer and a conversation, while the default keeps the skill's follow-ups and hand-offs one click away. The headless variant still carries the false stop report, since the skill prints no fixed line for the runner to read, and two variants are more to ship, test, and explain for an action whose two uses differ only in whether the person wants a follow-up; it depends on the action carrying a variant dropdown, which turns on the sibling question of where the action stands on the page.

open-question.question: A mission page of Gurita for VS Code is to list the mission's completed tasks, hidden by default behind one control that shows and hides them. Where does the list stand: inside the Remaining tasks pane, or in a pane of its own beside Open questions and Remaining tasks?
open-question.alternative: The completed tasks stand inside the existing Remaining tasks pane, beneath the remaining task list (and beneath its empty state when no task remains), behind one show/hide toggle that is collapsed by default; the page keeps its two pane headers, Open questions and Remaining tasks, under their current names, and the default-pane rule is unchanged. The smallest change to the page's structure: `PANES`, the header row, and the default-pane rule stay as they are, all task material sits in the one pane a reader already goes to for tasks, and the toggle alone carries the "hidden by default" requirement. The header "Remaining tasks" then names a pane that also holds completed work, and the list is reachable only after selecting that pane and scrolling past every remaining brief, so a mission with a long task list pushes the toggle far down; a finished mission's page, which has no remaining tasks, would have to reuse a pane whose name no longer fits it.

The completed tasks stand inside the second pane, beneath the remaining task list, behind one show/hide toggle collapsed by default, and that pane's header is renamed from "Remaining tasks" to a name covering both lists, such as "Tasks", with the remaining tasks heading their own part of it; the page keeps two pane headers and the default-pane rule. Keeps every task, remaining or completed, in one place with the two-header layout intact while removing the mismatch between the header and what the pane holds. Renames a label the extension shows today, its `aria-label`, its tests, the listing README, and the tracker's own wording ("Show each remaining task's brief" names the "Remaining tasks" pane), and the toggle still sits below every remaining brief, so the same scrolling cost as keeping the header remains.

The completed tasks get a pane of their own, a third header "Completed tasks" beside Open questions and Remaining tasks in the same row, the three of equal width filling the window; the pane header itself is the one control that shows and hides the list, which is hidden by default because the default-pane rule keeps opening on Open questions or Remaining tasks and never on the new pane, and the pane holds no further toggle. Reuses the page's existing show-one-pane mechanism rather than adding a new kind of control, keeps the Remaining tasks pane exactly what its name says, puts the list one click away whatever is shown, and gives a finished mission's page, which has neither open questions nor remaining tasks, a pane that fits it as it stands. Changes the page's fixed two-pane shape (`PANES`, `MissionPane`, the header row's equal-width split, the page tests) for a list most readers seldom open, narrows each header to a third of the width, and the remaining and completed tasks can never be seen side by side or on one scroll.

The completed tasks stand in a section of their own outside the two-pane area, drawn on every mission page whichever pane is selected, beneath the selected pane's content, behind one show/hide toggle collapsed by default; the two pane headers, their names, and the default-pane rule are unchanged. Reachable from either pane without switching, and leaves both the pane structure and the Remaining tasks pane untouched, so the history is a page-level fact about the mission rather than part of either pane. Breaks the page's layout rule that only the selected pane's content stands beneath the headers, and under Open questions it sits below a card of any length, so the toggle is found only by scrolling past unrelated content; it also adds one more always-drawn row to a page that already stacks the diagram, the recipe buttons, the preview, and the New task row.

open-question.question: Each completed task listed on a mission page of Gurita for VS Code is to carry a link to its `Task-completion:` commit. What does following the link open: the commit inside VS Code, and through which view or command, or the commit's page on the repository's remote host?
open-question.alternative: The link opens the commit inside VS Code only, as one read-only text document in an editor tab: the extension registers a content provider of its own scheme whose content is `git show <hash>` run through `execFile` from the project root, as the extension already runs `git log` and the missions tool, and opens it with the diff language, so the tab holds the subject, the verified bar as the body, and the whole patch, the brief among its removed lines. No remote host is involved and no other extension is called. It works for every commit the local repository holds, pushed or not, on any remote host or none, shows the subject, the bar, and the diff together as `tasks` and the commit record them, and adds no dependency beyond the `git` the extension already runs. The patch is one long plain diff with no per-file side-by-side view, no syntax highlighting of the changed files' own language, and no navigation between files, so a large task commit is hard to read there; the provider and its scheme are new code the extension has none of today.

The link opens the commit inside VS Code only, in VS Code's multi-file diff editor through the built-in `vscode.changes` command, titled by the task's heading, with one entry per file the commit changed, each comparing that file at `<hash>^` with the file at `<hash>`, both versions served by a content provider of the extension's own over `git show <rev>:<path>` and the file list read with `git show --name-status`. No remote host is involved and the built-in Git extension is not called. Each changed file reads as VS Code's own side-by-side diff, with the file's language highlighting and navigation between files, the richest in-editor view of the change, for every local commit whatever the remote. The commit's message and verified bar are not part of the diff editor, so the reader sees the change without the record beside it unless the page already shows the bar; it is the most code of the in-editor options (file list, added, deleted, and renamed files mapped to entries, two revisions per file).

The link opens the commit's page on the repository's remote host only, in the browser through `vscode.env.openExternal`: the extension reads the `origin` remote's URL, turns an SSH form such as `git@github.com:uHappyLogic/gurita.git` into its web address, and appends the host's commit path (`/commit/<hash>` on GitHub, `/-/commit/<hash>` on GitLab, `/commits/<hash>` on Bitbucket), with no link drawn where no remote is set or its host is not one the extension knows. Nothing opens inside VS Code. It is the smallest piece of code, and the host's commit page gives the full rendered commit, message, bar, and per-file diff, in the place a team already reviews and shares commits. A task completed and not yet pushed, the normal state while a mission runs locally, opens a not-found page; a repository with no remote, a self-hosted or unknown host, or a private repository the browser is not signed into gives no usable link, and the extension takes on a table of host URL formats.

Each completed task carries two links: the primary one opens the commit inside VS Code as the read-only `git show` text document of the extension's own scheme, and a second one, drawn only when the `origin` remote's host is one the extension knows, opens the commit's page on that host through `vscode.env.openExternal`, built as the remote-page option builds it. The in-editor link always works for any local commit while the remote link serves sharing and review on the host, so neither reader is left without a target. It is the code of both the text document and the remote URL mapping, a second control on every completed task's row, and a remote link that still opens a not-found page for an unpushed commit.

Each completed task carries two links: the primary one opens the commit inside VS Code in the multi-file diff editor through `vscode.changes`, served by the extension's own `git show <rev>:<path>` reads, and a second one, drawn only when the `origin` remote's host is one the extension knows, opens the commit's page on that host through `vscode.env.openExternal`. The reader gets VS Code's richest local view of the change and, where the host is known, the host's page with the commit's message and bar, covering both local reading and sharing. It carries the most code of any option (the diff editor's file mapping plus the host URL table), a second control on every row, the diff editor still shows no commit message or bar, and the remote link fails for an unpushed commit.

Each completed task carries one link whose target is chosen when it is followed: the commit's page on the remote host through `vscode.env.openExternal` when the `origin` remote's host is one the extension knows and the commit is reachable from a remote-tracking branch (`git branch -r --contains <hash>` prints a line), and otherwise the read-only `git show` text document inside VS Code. One control per row that never opens a not-found page: a pushed commit goes to the host's full page and an unpushed one, or one in a repository with no known host, still opens locally. The same link opens in two different places depending on push state the reader cannot see, which surprises; the remote-tracking check is only as fresh as the last fetch, and the code is that of both targets plus the check.

Each completed task carries one link whose target is chosen when it is followed: the commit's page on the remote host through `vscode.env.openExternal` when the `origin` remote's host is one the extension knows and the commit is reachable from a remote-tracking branch, and otherwise the multi-file diff editor inside VS Code through `vscode.changes`, served by the extension's own `git show <rev>:<path>` reads. One control per row that always opens something useful, the host's page for a pushed commit and VS Code's per-file side-by-side view for an unpushed one or where no host is known. The link's destination silently depends on push state, the local fallback shows no message or bar, and it carries the most moving parts of the single-link options (host URL table, remote-tracking check, diff editor file mapping).

open-question.question: In Gurita for VS Code an answer, a mission's goal, and a new task's issue description are to be typed into a box with room for several lines. Today each is asked through `vscode.window.showInputBox`, which holds one line, and the goal is asked from the side-bar view's rows, where no page stands. An earlier mission recorded that nothing is typed on a page anywhere in the extension. What provides the multi-line box?
open-question.alternative: The mission page draws the multi-line box itself: clicking Answer on a question card, or the New task row, opens a textarea with Run and Cancel in place on the page, under the card's head or the row, and the page posts the typed text to the host with the click instead of the host calling `askValues`. The goal, asked from the side-bar view's Define mission row where no page stands, is typed into a small dedicated webview panel the row opens as an editor tab, holding a goal textarea and the scope field, with Run and Cancel. The scope, the discussion note, and the Settings window's values stay in `vscode.window.showInputBox`. The answer and the issue are typed beside the question card or task list they concern, with the card's text in view while the user writes, which is the one place on the page the text belongs to. It reverses the recipe-variants mission's recorded decision that nothing is typed on a page and builds two input mechanisms, an inline one in `src/webview/page.ts` with its stand-in DOM tests and a separate goal panel with a webview script of its own, so the three values are asked in two different ways.

alternative.id: Inline page box, side-bar goal form

open-question.alternative: The mission page draws the multi-line box in place for the answer and the issue description, as a textarea with Run and Cancel under the clicked card's head or the New task row, posted to the host with the click. The goal is typed into a webview view added to the Gurita activity-bar container beside the native Missions tree, a form holding the goal textarea and the scope field that the Define mission row reveals and fills. The scope, the discussion note, and the Settings window's values stay in `vscode.window.showInputBox`. Defining a mission stays in the side bar where it is started, with no editor tab opened for it, while the per-mission values are typed on the page beside what they concern. It adds a second view to the container the activity-bar mission built as one native tree, a webview view with its own script, state, and tests, for a form used once per mission, and it still reverses the recorded no-typing-on-a-page decision with two input mechanisms; how it sits beside the view's notices depends on the axis the view-notice-form question owns.

One webview panel serves every multi-line value at all three sites: where `askValues` reaches the answer text, the goal, or the issue description, the host opens a small input panel as an editor tab holding one textarea, the value's prompt above it, and Run and Cancel, and resolves the value when Run is pressed or undefined when Cancel is pressed or the tab is closed, exactly as a dismissed input box does today. The mission page and the side-bar tree are unchanged, and the scope, the discussion note, and the Settings window's values stay in `vscode.window.showInputBox`. One mechanism behind the existing `askValues` call answers all three sites alike, the side-bar goal included, leaving the mission page's buttons-and-dropdowns-only drawing and its tests untouched. Each run opens and closes an extra editor tab that takes focus away from the mission page or tree, and the panel is a third webview script in the shared page shell, with its own message protocol and tests, built for a single textarea.

Every multi-line value at all three sites is typed in a VS Code text editor: where `askValues` reaches the answer text, the goal, or the issue description, the host opens an untitled Markdown document headed by the value's prompt as a comment, and the value is taken when the user fires a Start run action on the editor's title bar or a CodeLens, the prompt header stripped, and dropped as undefined when the document is closed unconfirmed. No webview gains an input, and the scope, the discussion note, and the Settings window's values stay in `vscode.window.showInputBox`. The user types in the full native editor, with its keybindings, undo, spell-check extensions, paste, and Markdown preview, and the extension adds no webview drawing at all, so the recorded rule that nothing is typed on a page holds unchanged. Confirming a value by a title-bar action or CodeLens and cancelling by closing a document is a convention the user must learn, an untitled document prompts to save on close unless the extension discards it itself, and the flow is driven through editor and document events that the `node:test` suite's stand-ins do not cover.

open-question.question: Gurita for VS Code is to gain a setting that closes a run's terminal by itself when its chain ran all its lines, while a chain that stopped keeps waiting for a keypress. Is the setting on or off by default?
open-question.alternative: The new setting ships off: every chain keeps printing its report and `Press any key to close this terminal.` and waiting for a keypress, as `runner.py`'s `wait_for_key` does today, until a user turns the setting on. Nothing changes for anyone who does not opt in: the end-of-run report a user has not yet read is never taken away without their choosing it, the behaviour the first-version mission built on purpose stays the default, and `scripts/capture_demo.js`, which waits for `Press any key to close this terminal.` in a throwaway profile running on defaults, keeps working as it is. The pain the tracker entry names stays the default experience: a successful chain still leaves the mission's page disabled until someone presses a key, so a user who never finds the setting gains nothing from it, and most users never open settings for an extension.

The new setting ships on: a chain that ran all its lines closes its terminal by itself and unblocks the mission's page, while a chain that stopped keeps waiting for a keypress; a user who wants every terminal to stay open turns the setting off. Every user gets the fix the tracker entry asks for without looking for it: a successful run unblocks its page at once, the common case costs no keypress, and the terminal stays open exactly when there is something to read, a stop. A successful chain's report and the transcript above it vanish the moment it ends, which changes the extension's established behaviour for every existing user in 0.3.0 and loses output that a user who looked away never saw; `scripts/capture_demo.js` must write the setting off into its profile's `settings.json` (or wait on something other than the keypress line) before the demo can be re-captured.

The setting's default is not one value for every chain: with the setting left untouched, a chain whose lines are all headless closes its terminal when it ran all its lines, and a chain holding an interactive line keeps waiting for a keypress (the runner already tells the two kinds apart through `line_kind`); the setting takes explicit values that override this for every chain, so it becomes a choice of more than on and off. Closes by itself where no one is at the terminal to press a key, the long unattended headless chains that block a page longest, while leaving unchanged the interactive chains, where the user is at the terminal anyway and the keypress costs nothing. A default that depends on what a chain holds is harder to describe in the setting's description and harder to predict from a button, the setting stops being a plain boolean, and the output it discards by default is exactly that of the unattended chains, whose report the absent user has not read.

The setting ships with no value chosen: the first time a chain runs all its lines with the setting unset, the terminal waits for a keypress as today and the extension asks once, through a notification, whether such terminals should close by themselves from now on, storing the answer as the setting's value; until answered, it behaves as off. Every user meets the choice at the moment it matters and decides it knowingly, so the fix is discovered without anyone's established behaviour being changed silently. Adds a prompt and a third, unset state to code and tests for a one-bit preference, interrupts the very first successful run with a notification, and leaves the setting's documented default ambiguous; dismissing the notification without answering leaves the blocking behaviour in place.

open-question.question: The runner of Gurita for VS Code waits for a keypress after every chain and after every looped task run. A new setting is to close the terminal by itself when a chain ran all its lines. Does the setting also close the terminal of a looped task run that completed every task?
open-question.alternative: The one new setting governs both kinds of run. With it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` (the runner's `finished` outcome, reached once no `##` heading is left in `TASKS_TODO.md`) prints its report and exits without waiting for a keypress, so its terminal closes and the page unblocks. A loop that stopped (an unresolved assignment, a task that did not end on `Task completed.`, or an unreadable task list) still waits for a keypress, as a stopped chain does. One rule for every run: `run_chain` and `run_loop` already end the same way (report, `wait_for_key`, exit 0 when finished), so the setting skips the same wait at both, and the looped run, which is the long unattended run where an unblocked page on success matters most, gets the benefit too. The loop's closing report (`Tasks completed: N`) and every task session's output vanish with the terminal on success, leaving only the commits and the refreshed page as the record; the setting's description and the README must say it reaches looped runs, since the tracker entry names only chains.

The setting closes only a chain's terminal. A looped task run keeps waiting for a keypress after its report whatever the setting says and however the loop ended, exactly as today. Follows the tracker entry's wording literally and keeps the one run that can complete many tasks unattended always reviewable at its end, with the runner's loop path left unchanged. A loop that completed every task still leaves the mission's page blocked until someone presses a key, the very wait the setting exists to remove, and a user who turned the setting on is likely to read the loop's lingering terminal as the setting not working.

Looped runs get a setting of their own beside the chain one: with it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` exits without waiting for a keypress, while a stopped loop still waits; the chain setting does not reach loops and the loop setting does not reach chains. Lets a user auto-close short chains while still reviewing the output of a long multi-task run, or the reverse, without either choice being forced on the other. Adds a second setting to the manifest, its description, and the README for a distinction few users are likely to want, and needs a default of its own, which depends on how the default of the chain setting is settled.

open-question.question: Gurita for VS Code is to re-read the missions when git state changes through a commit, a pull, or a branch switch made outside its own runs; today its one file watcher covers the mission documents only. How does the extension learn of such a change: by watching files inside the repository's `.git` directory, or through the API of VS Code's built-in Git extension?

The harness check of Gurita for VS Code covers Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex, reporting for each whether its CLI is found, whether a Gurita copy is installed, and whether that copy is at least the packaged version. The Missions side-bar view is to say when the check fails. Which results make the view say so: a failure of any harness, of every harness, or only of the harnesses that are enabled or whose CLI is found?

The harness check of Gurita for VS Code first runs in a session when the Settings window opens, and its result is kept for the session. Once the Missions side-bar view is to show a missing or outdated plugin, when does the check first run?
open-question.alternative: The check first runs in the background as soon as the Missions view first draws in a session (in practice at activation, which `onView:gurita.missions` triggers), through the same `checkHarnesses` path the Settings window uses, and its result stays kept for the rest of the session as today: only the Settings window's Check again and the end of an install or update run run it afresh, and the view's Refresh does not. A person who has just installed the extension is told the plugin is missing or outdated without opening anything or firing a run, which is exactly the case the tracker entry names, and the check still runs at most once per session unless asked, as the Settings window's design already holds. Every session in which the view is shown spends one `harness_check.py` run, a login-shell session listing up to three CLIs with a 120-second limit, even when the plugin is fine and the person never looks at the result; and a plugin installed or updated outside the extension (from a terminal) leaves a stale notice standing until Check again in Settings or a window reload.

alternative.id: At first draw, again on Refresh

open-question.alternative: The check first runs in the background as soon as the Missions view first draws in a session, as in the previous option, and the premise that its result is kept for the whole session is relaxed: besides Check again and the end of an install or update run, the view's Refresh command (`gurita.refreshMissions`, which already re-reads everything else) also runs it afresh, the result replacing the kept one for the view and the Settings window alike. The notice is shown just as early, and a person who fixed the plugin outside the extension can clear or confirm it from the view itself with the Refresh they already use, so the view never holds a result the person has no way to renew from where it is shown. Refresh gains a slow, shell-spawning side effect it does not have today, so a Refresh pressed to re-read the missions also starts a check of up to a couple of minutes, and the Settings window's stated rule that no refresh or re-read runs the check, recorded in `settingsWindow.ts`, has to be rewritten.

The check does not run at activation or view draw; it first runs when the person fires the session's first run of a recipe or button from a mission page or the side-bar view (or opens the Settings window, as today, whichever comes first), and its result is then kept for the session as today and shown in the view from then on. No check is spent in a session where nothing is run, and the result arrives at the one moment the tracker entry says a missing plugin hurts, the first run, so the view can say why that run is failing rather than leaving the terminal to say it. A newcomer still sees only `No mission is live.` until they fire something, so the view gives no warning before the first failure, only an explanation beside it; and either the first run waits seconds for the check or both start together and the run fails anyway.

The check runs automatically only where it does today, on the Settings window's first opening; the Missions view, until a check has run in the session, offers a control to check the plugin install, which runs the check through the same path, the result then kept for the session and shown in the view. No background process is ever started without the person asking, so startup cost and the CLIs' login-shell sessions stay exactly as they are, while the view still gives a newcomer a visible first step towards the install state. The person must notice and choose the control before learning anything, so the newcomer the entry describes can still skip it and meet the failure in the terminal first; it also needs a place in the view for the control, which depends on the form the View notice form question gives the view's notices.

open-question.question: The Missions side-bar view of Gurita for VS Code is a native tree that shows `No mission is live.` through the tree view's message. It is to show two new things: a notice that the plugin is missing or outdated, linking to the Settings window, and an offer to run the workflow bootstrap. In what form does the view show them: as tree rows, as the view's welcome content, in the view's message, or as notifications?
open-question.alternative: Both are tree rows: a plugin notice row (warning icon, label saying the plugin is missing or outdated, its click opening the Settings window) and a bootstrap offer row (its click running `init-mission-base-workflow`), each present only while its condition holds and standing at the top of the tree, above New mission and Define mission. The view's message keeps only `No mission is live.` and the read-failure line, and no notification is shown. It fits the view as it is built: `missionTree.ts` already draws every action as a leaf row with a command, an icon, and a tooltip, so each new thing is one more row kind, persistent while its condition holds, clickable, and working in every state of the view, with or without live missions. A warning drawn as a row looks like one more action among New mission and the mission rows and is easier to scroll past than a distinct banner, and two conditional rows grow the top of a tree that already opens with two fixed rows.

Both are the view's welcome content, contributed under `viewsWelcome` with Markdown text and command links (a link opening the Settings window, a button running the bootstrap), each entry keyed by a `when` context the extension sets. Because welcome content is drawn only while the tree holds no row, the tree returns no rows at all, the mission-starting rows and the mission rows included, while either condition holds, and draws them again once both clear. No notification is shown. Welcome content is VS Code's own form for an onboarding state: it renders real links and full-width buttons, and with the tree emptied the notice is the only thing in the view, impossible to miss on a fresh install. Emptying the tree hides New mission, Define mission, and every live mission while the bootstrap is not yet run or while the check fails, so a project whose context file lacks the section, or whose check fails for a harness the user never runs, loses the view's whole use until the condition clears; the contributed text is fixed in the manifest, so the notice cannot name which harness or version failed.

The plugin notice is welcome content: while the check fails the tree returns no rows and the welcome content shows the notice with a link to the Settings window, plus the bootstrap button when the section is also missing. While the check passes, the bootstrap offer is a tree row at the top of the tree, present only while the section is missing, and the message keeps its two lines. No notification is shown. The view is emptied only in the state where its runs would fail anyway, a missing or outdated plugin, so the strongest form is spent on the blocking problem while the non-blocking bootstrap offer leaves the missions in view. The view switches between two layouts, so the bootstrap offer moves from a welcome button to a row depending on the check, and two mechanisms (manifest `when` contexts and a row kind) must be kept in step; it also hides the starting rows on a check failure, whose scope is the sibling question on which harnesses count.

The plugin notice is plain text in the view's `message`, joined with or replacing `No mission is live.`, telling the user to open Settings through the view's existing Settings title-bar icon, since the message carries no link. The bootstrap offer is a tree row at the top of the tree, present only while the section is missing. No notification is shown. The message already stands above the tree as the view's one status line, so a notice there reads as a status rather than an action and costs no new row, no manifest contribution, and no change to the tree's rows. `TreeView.message` is a plain string with no link or button, so the notice cannot link to the Settings window as the tracker asks and only points at the gear icon, and it must share the one message with `No mission is live.` and the read-failure line.

Both are notifications: a warning notification saying the plugin is missing or outdated with an Open Settings button, and an information notification offering the bootstrap with a Run button, each shown once per session when its condition is found. The view itself gains no row, welcome content, or message. A notification reaches the user even while the side-bar view is closed or another view is focused, which is the case on a fresh install, and needs no change to the tree. Notifications are transient and easily dismissed or silenced, so once closed the view still shows only `No mission is live.`, the state the tracker entry calls the problem; when the notification appears is bound to the sibling question on when the check first runs.

The plugin notice is a warning notification with an Open Settings button, shown once per session when the check fails, and the bootstrap offer is a tree row at the top of the tree, present only while the section is missing. The view's message keeps its two lines. The urgent, blocking problem gets the form that interrupts and reaches the user outside the view, while the standing offer stays where the user starts work, in the view. Once the notification is dismissed the view says nothing about the failed check, so the view itself does not show the failure as the tracker entry asks; its moment depends on the sibling question on when the check first runs.

The plugin notice is a tree row at the top of the tree, present while the check fails, its click opening the Settings window. The bootstrap offer is an information notification with a Run button, shown once per session while the section is missing, and the view gains no bootstrap row.
